guide](https://health.usnews.com/best-diet/medication/top-glp-1-weight-loss-medication-providers#comparison) The surging popularity of [weight loss medications](https://health.usnews.com/conditions/prescription-weight-loss-drugs) like Ozempic, [Wegovy](https://health.usnews.com/wellness/articles/do-weight-loss-products-like-wegovy-help-weight-loss), Zepbound and [Mounjaro](https://health.usnews.com/wellness/articles/mounjaro-weight-loss), known as GLP-1 agonists, has fueled a boom in telehealth services specializing in obesity medicine. These online providers offer a convenient, discreet and often more affordable way to access these powerful drugs, sidestepping traditional in-person doctor visits. Today, there are dozens of online providers that prescribe GLP-1s. However, the rapid growth of this market – which includes established wellness brands like WeightWatchers and Noom to newer, no-frills platforms like SkinnyRx and Sprout – has created a confusing landscape for consumers. What sets these companies apart is how they structure their services and their approach to care. Some providers offer [insurance support](https://health.usnews.com/best-diet/medication/articles/navigating-insurance-coverage-for-glp-1-medications-a-step-by-step-guide) for brand name medications, such as [Ozempic](https://health.usnews.com/wellness/articles/is-ozempic-safe-and-effective-for-weight-loss) and [Zepbound](https://health.usnews.com/wellness/article/zepbound-for-weight-loss), while others focus on lower-cost compounded medications that are not approved by the Food and Drug Administration. Programs also vary significantly in clinical quality, with some offering specialized dosing and adjustments, regular check-ins and unlimited communication with a healthcare team to manage common [side effects](https://health.usnews.com/best-diet/medication/articles/glp-1-side-effects-expert-tips-to-manage-nausea-constipation-and-weight-loss-fatigue). Some include baseline and regular blood work, whereas others may require patients to obtain labs separately, or not at all. Additionally, the best online GLP-1 providers programs offer the necessary behavioral and [nutritional support](https://health.usnews.com/wellness/food/articles/what-to-eat-and-avoid-on-semaglutide) vital for successful long-term weight management. To help you make an informed choice, we evaluated 23 of the most popular online GLP-1 medication providers, detailing the pros, cons and essential program features of each one. Insurance concierge services and support** Many brand-name medications will require a [prior authorization from your health insurance](https://health.usnews.com/best-diet/medication/articles/navigating-insurance-coverage-for-glp-1-medications-a-step-by-step-guide). Some providers will do the footwork for you and contact the [insurance company](https://health.usnews.com/medicare/articles/does-medicare-cover-ozempic) to get this medication approved, while other providers only accept direct payment from the consumer. Some providers will also accept flexible spending accounts or health savings accounts as payment. ### **2\. Medication options** Many medications are available for weight loss, including brand name GLP-1s and compounded versions. Brand name injectable options include Ozempic, Mounjaro, Saxenda, Trulicity, Victoza, Wegovy and Zepbound. Brand name oral options include, Foundayo (orforglipron), Rybelsus and [Wegovy](https://health.usnews.com/best-diet/medication/articles/what-to-know-about-the-new-wegovy-pill). Compounded versions include [semaglutide or tirzepatide](https://health.usnews.com/best-diet/medication/articles/semaglutide-vs-tirzepatide) and may be available as an injectable, pill or sublingual oral formulation. A generic liraglutide injection is also available. For providers that offer compounded GLP-1 options, it's important to confirm the company follows proper quality control and safety measures. Compounding pharmacies should be able to provide a Certificate of Analysis, which verifies the product has been tested for safety and quality and follows proper regulations. It is also important to use a compounding pharmacy that has been accredited by either the Pharmacy Compounding Accreditation Board or the National Association of Boards of Pharmacy. Pharmacies with these accreditations have received proper training and meet rigorous quality and safety standards. ### **3\. Delivery** How you receive your prescription will depend on the provider. Providers that offer compounded medications typically work with compounding pharmacies that ship your medication directly to you. Some providers also have partnerships with drug manufacturers, such as Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk, which may also ship your medication directly to you. If you are using insurance for a brand-name medication, your prescription can be picked up at your local pharmacy. ### **4\. Support beyond the script** Proper care involves being able to easily get in touch with your health care provider. Some GLP-1 providers offer regular check-ins and appointments, while others may provide little to no support via chat. In some cases, you may only be able to contact your care team through messaging and may not hear back for several days. You may also be required to show proof of weight loss before your refill is approved, especially if you are using insurance. Providers may offer side effects management, which can include dose adjustment, counseling and anti-nausea medication. Some plans may also include access to and support from fitness coaches, nutritionists or registered dietitians. ### **5\. Cost** Pricing structures vary by program. Some providers offer flat monthly fees for medications, while others increase the price as the dosage rises. In addition to medication costs, consider whether providers charge extra for monthly membership fees or consultations. Some require an additional monthly appointment fee to access a provider. If the program accepts insurance, the membership fee often includes insurance concierge service that helps submit prior authorizations or otherwise attempt to obtain medical coverage. Several providers offer a more holistic approach to weight loss, which may include meal plans and recipes, food tracking, workouts, educational content and community support. Other services strictly focus on prescribing the prescription and not much more. ### **6\. Clinical rigor** It's important to choose a program that is both knowledgeable and prioritizes safety. Lab testing before starting weight loss medication can ensure there are no underlying health conditions or restrictions to treatment. While some programs provide lab testing with the monthly fee, others do not cover the costs or require them. Before beginning treatment with a GLP-1 receptor agonist, providers may order lab work to evaluate overall health and rule out conditions that could contribute to weight gain. Labs are often repeated about every six months or sooner if problematic side effects occur. Common tests include a comprehensive metabolic panel, which shows how well the kidneys and liver are functioning. Monitoring these levels can show if the medication is improving kidney and liver health and not causing complications. Hemoglobin A1C measures blood sugar levels over the previous three months and can help identify [diabetes](https://health.usnews.com/conditions/diabetes) or [prediabetes](https://health.usnews.com/conditions/diabetes/prediabetes) if levels are higher. [Cholesterol testing](https://health.usnews.com/health-care/patient-advice/articles/how-to-track-your-cholesterol) helps determine your risk of heart disease and stroke, and these medications often improve cholesterol levels and overall health. Providers may also check thyroid levels, since thyroid conditions can contribute to weight gain. ### **7\. Approval process** Most weight loss medication programs work by asking patients to share basic information like their height, weight, body mass index and medical history. Some providers have a quick, simple process that involves completing a questionnaire, uploading identification or a photo and briefly chatting with a healthcare provider. Others may require a one-on-one video appointment with a health care provider and lab testing before prescribing medication. You Need to Know The sudden surge in prescribing GLP-1s led to nationwide drug shortages in 2022. This, along with the high cost of these meds, opened the door for compounding pharmacies as an alternative. Although the GLP-1 drug shortage ended in 2025, compounding pharmacies continue to produce these medications. Many companies offer specialized dosage forms – or [microdosing options](https://health.usnews.com/wellness/articles/can-microdosing-weight-loss-drugs-like-ozempic-help-you-lose-weight), which involve starting with very small doses and gradually increasing them – for a more personalized approach. As of April 2026, the FDA has officially proposed removing semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide from the 503B bulks list. This means large-scale compounding is now restricted because the FDA considers the shortages resolved. Several major compounding labs (like ProRx and BPI Labs) ceased production in early 2026. A public comment period is now open through June 29, 2026 until a final decision is made. The FDA permits the use of a compounded drug only when the medical need cannot be met by an FDA-approved drug or when an approved product is unavailable due to drug shortages. Compounded medications are not generic versions and are not FDA-approved. Unlike approved drugs, they have not been tested for safety, effectiveness or quality control. In fact, the FDA has issued warning letters to several online telehealth companies regarding false and misleading information about GLP-1 medications. When seeking out an online company for telehealth medicine, it's important to research before you buy. The following are red flags to look for when considering getting GLP-1s online. ### **Red Flag No. 1: Asynchronous interactions** Many online companies don't require a video visit before prescribing GLP-1s. You will be required to fill out an online questionnaire and have the ability to chat about the [questions you have](https://health.usnews.com/wellness/articles/questions-to-ask-your-doctor-before-starting-a-glp-1-weight-loss-drug). While this model allows for quick, easily accessible care, it's important that you get high-quality care and management of your condition. Dr. Kevin Gendreau, a dual board-certified family and obesity medicine physician with Signature Healthcare in Massachusetts, says that your telehealth visit should feel like a real visit in a doctor's office, where the provider has a plan for accountability and ongoing follow-up care. ### **Red flag No. 2: Lack of lab testing** Lab testing is essential for discovering underlying medical conditions, such as hypothyroidism or diabetes, and for getting a picture of a person's whole health. It can also indicate how your kidneys, [heart](https://health.usnews.com/best-diet/medication/articles/glp-1-drugs-for-heart-health-benefits-side-effects-who-should-take-them) and liver are functioning. Gendreau recommends checking bloodwork at the beginning of treatment and again in six months. “By staying on top of this data, we can catch potential issues like muscle loss or dehydration early, rather than reacting to them once symptoms arise.” He also notes that potential problems, such as fatty liver disease, can be detected and monitored to see if weight loss improves these conditions. Another benefit is individualizing the treatment plan to maximize results while minimizing side effects and risk. ### **Red flag No. 3: Lack of quality control or testing by the pharmacy** Compounding medications are not FDA-approved and are regulated differently. Dr. Jennifer Brown, a board-certified obesity medicine doctor, states that compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide don't have the rigorous safety data that the FDA-approved versions do. If you plan on using a compounded medication, it’s important to do some research, particularly to ensure the pharmacy follows proper safety and quality standards. Reputable compounding pharmacies should provide documentation that their product has been tested and meets quality, safety and regulatory standards. This is known as a Certificate of Analysis, or CoA. When choosing a pharmacy, it's important to ensure that the pharmacy is accredited by the Pharmacy Compounding Accreditation Board. The PCAB accreditation ensures that pharmacies and their staff have proper training, follow quality control measures and have contamination prevention procedures in place. ### **A Note Regarding Compounded GLP-1s** Compounded drugs are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
